metadata.title: Miami University president among 503 rescued from grounded liner, 11 December 1937
metadata.transcript:
[page 1]
Miami U. [University] President Among 503 Rescued From Grounded Liner

Dr. [Doctor] Upham, Wife and Daughter Taken From Hoover

BELIEVED SAFE

Several Passengers May Be Suffering of Exposure

By the United Press.

Dr. Alfred H. Upham, president of Miami University, Oxford, O. [Ohio], Mrs. [married woman] Upham and their daughter, Peggy Lou, 26, were among 503 passengers rescued Saturday from the liner President Hoover, aground on a reef off Formosa [Taiwan] in the Pacific, 400 miles south of Japan.

Dr. Upham, enjoying his first vacation in 10 years, had been on a tour of the orient.

The Uphams left Oxford Nov. [November] 17 and were to return in mid-April.

The family was believed safe, although reports from the stricken $8,000,000 liner said the ship's physician, Dr. William Park, had set up an emergency hospital on [unclear] Island, where the passengers were taken. It was assumed the passengers were suffering from exposure.

Friends and relatives of Dr. and Mrs. Upham at Oxford expressed hope today that the Uphams were not aboard the liner. Dr. Upham's itinerary called for a two-week visit to Yokohoma [Yokohama], Japan. The last word heard from him was that he had landed safely at Yokohoma [Yokohama], Dec. [December] 6. It is believed, however, Dr. Upham may have changed his mind due to unsettled conditions in the Orient and sailed to Tokyo [Japan].

Seas Are Heavy

Radio advices indicated heavy seas had made difficult the transferring of the passengers and salvage efforts to refloat the 38,800-ton Dollar liner, which figured in the news when it was bombed by Chinese planes off Shanghai early in the Sino-Japanese war.

The President Hoover's sister ship, the President McKinley, racing to the scene under full steam, was expected to arrive at dusk. It was believed the ship's cargo would have to be jettisoned before it could be refloated.

The liner was aground about 30 miles off Formosa, the chief island of the group. One of the last messages asked for all possible salvage aid. Presumably her crew of 330 remained aboard. Capt. [Captain] George Yardley, commander of the liner, reported that there was no immediate danger.

The German steamer Preussen was standing by.

Swell on Reef Blamed

No storms were reported in the area. It was assumed that the boiling seas was caused by the natural swell of the sea over the reef.

The accident occurred Friday night while the President Hoover was plying a strange route, avoiding the area of the Sino-Japanese war. That was the only available explanation for the grounding.

The destroyers Alden from Manila, about 500 miles away, and Barker from Olongapo, 50 miles northwest of Manila, were sent to the scene at full speed. The Canadian Pacific liner Empress of Asia also was on its way. The naval vessels were due to arrive first. The Hoover sailed from San Francisco Nov. 22.

Ordinarily, the President Hoover went from Kobe to Shanghai, but the Chinese port was omitted because of the war.

RESCUED FROM LINER

Dr. Alfred H. Upham
